method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

items.setting: A volunteer shed at the campus botanical garden; the volunteer coordinator is speaking to a student volunteer who has just come in.

worlds.line: Could you carry these seedling trays out to the north beds?
worlds.reply: Sure — I'll take two at a time so nothing tips.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The coordinator asks for hands-on help moving trays, so agreeing and describing how they'll be carried is exactly the cooperative answer. Sympathy about ruined orchid cuttings responds to a loss nobody reported. Relief about a second potting bench answers an announcement that was never made, and naming a shelf behind the twine answers a location question that was never asked.

kills.1: The line says "carry these seedling" trays out — it hands over a task, and nothing in it reports anything lost, so mourning cuttings has nothing to attach to.
kills.2: The line only points to "the north beds" as a destination; no new equipment for the shed is announced, so welcoming extra bench space fits nothing said.
kills.3: "Could you carry" asks for an action, not for information, so answering with which shelf something sits on ignores the request entirely.

worlds.line: The greenhouse heater failed overnight, so the orchid cuttings are gone.
worlds.reply: That's awful — those cuttings took the whole spring to root.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A heater failure that killed the cuttings calls for shared dismay, and noting how long they took to root shows the volunteer grasps the size of the loss. Agreeing to carry trays two at a time accepts a job that was never offered. Welcoming a new potting bench treats a setback as a gain, and naming a shelf answers no question here.

kills.0: Because the line reports that "the orchid cuttings" are dead, it makes no request; promising to carry trays carefully accepts an instruction that was never given.
kills.2: "heater failed overnight" reports damage, not a purchase or a grant, so relief about crowding at a new bench answers nothing in it.
kills.3: The line closes with the cuttings "are gone" — a statement, not a search, so supplying a shelf location has no question to answer.

worlds.line: The garden club funded a second potting bench for this shed.
worlds.reply: Finally — we won't be elbowing each other every Saturday.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Funding for a second bench solves a crowding problem the volunteers live with, so naming that relief is the natural reaction. Agreeing to carry trays takes on work that was never assigned. Grieving lost cuttings misreads good news as a disaster, and pointing to a shelf answers a question the coordinator never raised.

kills.0: The line announces a "second potting bench" arriving; it asks for nothing, so a promise about tipping trays responds to an instruction that isn't there.
kills.1: The club "funded a second" bench — that's a gain for the shed, so treating the moment as a loss to console contradicts what was said.
kills.3: The news is "for this shed" in general; no missing item is being hunted, so naming a shelf and a green tin answers no one.

worlds.line: Do you know which shelf the labeled seed envelopes ended up on?
worlds.reply: Right — third one down, behind the twine, in the green tin.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The coordinator is hunting for the seed envelopes, so the useful reply is the exact shelf and container. Promising to carry trays two at a time accepts a task nobody assigned. Sorrow over dead cuttings and delight about a new bench both react to news that this line never delivers.

kills.0: The line asks about "the labeled seed envelopes" and requests no physical work, so agreeing to carry trays without tipping them answers a request that was never made.
kills.1: "Do you know" opens a question, not a report of damage, so an expression of sympathy for lost cuttings has nothing to console.
kills.2: Asking "which shelf" something sits on announces nothing new for the shed, so celebrating extra bench space responds to news that wasn't given.

items.setting: At the dorm bike repair stand outside the residence hall, a student and the bike-shop volunteer on duty.

worlds.line: Your back tire's flat again — the patch didn't hold overnight.
worlds.reply: Then I'll just buy a new tube this time.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The volunteer reports that the repair failed, so abandoning patches for a whole new tube is the obvious next move. Relief about a wobble answers a wheel that was straightened, which never happened here. Saying when to let go answers a request for hands, and a promise about five-thirty answers a closing time, neither of which was raised.

kills.1: "the patch didn't hold" reports a failure, so there is nothing fixed to be relieved about and no wobble was ever straightened.
kills.2: "Your back tire's" is a diagnosis I'm handing you, not a job I need hands for, so telling me to say when helps nothing.
kills.3: "flat again" says nothing about closing time, so a promise to finish by five-thirty answers a deadline I never set.

worlds.keyAct: expresses relief at a fixed problem
worlds.line: I trued your wheel this morning and it's spinning perfectly straight.
worlds.reply: That's a relief — I've been riding that wobble for weeks.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A wheel that now spins straight explains weeks of wobble ending, so relief is exactly right. Buying a tube treats the news as a flat tire, which was never mentioned. Offering to keep something from rolling assumes work still in progress, and finishing by five-thirty assumes a deadline.

kills.0: "trued your wheel" is finished work, so buying a new tube answers a tire failure I never reported.
kills.2: "this morning" puts the job in the past, so offering to steady anything for me arrives far too late.
kills.3: "spinning perfectly straight" is a result, not a rule about hours, so a promise about five-thirty attaches to nothing.

worlds.keyAct: agrees and asks for a cue
worlds.line: Can you hold the frame steady while I tighten this bolt?
worlds.reply: Say when — I'll keep it from rolling forward.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The volunteer needs a second pair of hands right now, so agreeing and asking for the cue fits. Buying a tube leaves the frame unheld and answers no request. Relief about a wobble responds to completed work, and a promise about five-thirty responds to a closing rule.

kills.0: "hold the frame steady" asks for help this minute, so announcing a tube purchase leaves my hands still full.
kills.1: "tighten this bolt" is work still underway, so calling something a weeks-long relief fits nothing I said.
kills.3: "Can you hold" is a request for the next minute, not a closing rule, so five-thirty is beside the point.

worlds.line: All the stand's tools go back on the board by six.
worlds.reply: I'll be done by five-thirty and put things away.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: A stated cutoff invites a commitment to finish before it, which is what this reply gives. Buying a tube answers a tire diagnosis that was never made. Relief about a wobble answers a completed repair, and asking for a cue answers a request for hands.

kills.0: "go back on the board" is about tools, not tires, so buying a tube answers a problem I never raised.
kills.1: "the stand's tools" are shop property, so relief about weeks of wobble responds to a repair I never mentioned.
kills.2: "by six" sets a deadline rather than asking for hands, so telling me to say when answers a request I didn't make.

worlds.reply: No wonder it looked empty — let me change the date.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Being shown the wrong date explains why the grid looked so open, and changing it is the fix. Returning at nine responds to rooms being full, which I said nothing about. Accepting a list place accepts an offer, and naming the party answers a question.
